analysis.one_liner: Restores corporate excise taxes on oil and chemical companies to fund toxic waste cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote after being referred there in July 2014.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. Since its dedicated cleanup fund ran dry in the 1990s, ordinary taxpayers have been paying for those cleanups out of general revenue instead of the companies that created the pollution. This bill would bring back the expired taxes on oil, petroleum products, and industrial chemicals that used to fill that fund, raise the oil rate, and make the fund's money available for cleanups without needing yearly approval from Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities living near hazardous waste sites, who get a dedicated, growing source of cleanup money, and taxpayers generally, who would stop covering cleanup costs that polluting industries previously paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, which had applied only to periods ending in 1995 or earlier, beginning 60 days after enactment.
It raises the rate from 9.7 cents to 15.8 cents per barrel of crude oil and adjusts it, and the per-ton chemical taxes, for inflation going forward.
It expands the definition of taxed crude oil to include oil from tar sands and oil shale, closing a gap in the old tax.
It makes money in the Hazardous Substance Superfund available for environmental cleanup without further congressional appropriations, so the fund works as intended rather than sitting idle.
It reinstates and increases per-ton taxes on taxable chemicals such as benzene, mercury, lead oxide, and arsenic compounds, whose production historically contributed to Superfund pollution.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, and chemical manufacturers, who pay the new and higher excise taxes; some of the oil tax would likely be passed through to consumers in small increments per barrel of gasoline.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax on crude oil is largely passed through into fuel prices, so consumers would pay a small share of it at the pump, though the per-barrel amount is modest.
The tax applies to all oil and petroleum products received or entered, not just from companies with Superfund liabilities, so the burden is not perfectly matched to who polluted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is a modest per-barrel and per-ton tax concentrated on industries whose products and byproducts created the toxic sites; the benefit is dedicated funding to clean up contaminated land and water near communities. The main honest objection is the fuel-price passthrough, which is small relative to the cleanup benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on July 29, 2014, with Senators Menendez and Boxer joining as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was its last action of record.
The Finance Committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, and the Congress expired on January 3, 2015 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and chemical companies are better off because the bill died, since they avoided reinstated and higher excise taxes, and taxpayers continue paying Superfund cleanup costs from general revenue.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Robert Menendez and Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill for the remainder of the 113th Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: American Chemistry Council and allied petrochemical interests
against.what_they_did: Long opposed reinstating the expired Superfund excise taxes on the industry.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: The bill would tax their crude oil at 15.8 cents per barrel and newly include tar sands and oil shale oil in the tax base, and inflation would raise the rate further over time. Their interest in avoiding the tax runs against taxpayers, who otherwise fund Superfund cleanups.
The bill would reinstate and increase per-ton federal excise taxes on dozens of taxable chemicals, from benzene to mercury. The industry has historically opposed these taxes as an added input cost.

Refiners would collect and remit the tax, and much of it would pass through to gasoline prices in small amounts per barrel, a modest cost to drivers that funds cleanup of contamination near communities.
A funded Superfund means more government-financed cleanup work, which benefits the contractors who perform it while removing toxic waste from communities.
